projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Raymond C. Peer was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: This is Gary Swanson with Americans Remembered, interviewing Raymond C. Peer, "Shine" as he's known to all those who know and love him, at his home in Gardner, Kansas, on December 4, 2003. Shine served in the US Army during World War II, and then in the Navy here in the United States until he had 20 years service. His experience in World War II as a sergeant was with the 713th Railway Battalion. He served from July 1941 to August 1945, and again from 1947 to 1963, here in the United States in the Navy. He's the holder of the European-African-Middle East Medal, the European Campaign, the Victory Medal, Eastern Theater Medal, the Good Conduct Medal. He was born on July 18, 1915. Shine, where did you grow up as a kid?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Edgerton, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Edgerton, that's just a few miles from where we're sitting?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were you on a farm or in town or --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: In town.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Lived in town. What did your daddy do to feed the family?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: He worked on a railroad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: He worked on the railroad. Where, in Edgerton or --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: In Edgerton.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: In Edgerton. Was your mom a stay-at-home mom?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How many kids did the family have?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We had five boys and a girl.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Five boys and a girl. And were you the oldest? Youngest? Where were you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: I'm next to the youngest.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You were the next to the youngest of five boys and a girl raised by a stay-at-home mom, of course, back then --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and your daddy worked on the railroad in Edgerton. How many of the six children are still living? One --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Me.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- Shine. We're talking to the man?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, was it just kind of an ordinary childhood? Did you enjoy growing up in Edgerton?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yes. I had little league baseball, and Babe Ruth. I played semi-pro ball myself.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: When I was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, that's good. So when Pearl Harbor happened, you were -- well, you'd already been in the service --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- before Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you got -- what did you do between the time you left school and you got in the Army?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, we -- when they put the call to war ____, we helped load the trucks and stuff to get them out to going.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: I see, that's what you did --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- as a civilian, and then you got drafted?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Then you got drafted, so you went in the service. Actually, you went in before we were at war?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You went in July of 1941?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right. I was in about a year or so before.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Where did you get sworn in --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: As a matter of fact, that's -- we trained out at Clovis, New Mexico.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Clovis, New Mexico. Okay. Where did you get sworn into the Army? Where did they induct you, at Fort Leavenworth?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, Fort Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then they put you on a train --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- to go to Clovis to basic?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Basic, yeah, and Clovis, New Mexico, that's where we shipped out of.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: I see --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: In Clovis.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How many of your -- you had five brothers and a sister?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did any of your other brothers serve in the war?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: My oldest brother did. He was chief warrant officer.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. You had one in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And that's all.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And both you guys -- both you boys came back safely?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Wonderful. Was he the first one to go, or were you the first one to go?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: He was first. He was first to go.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Do you remember the day you left home to go to the Army? Do you remember talking to your mom and dad and telling them goodbye?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, no, I just -- I just remember we got on a train and went to ...

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Clovis?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Clovis.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So they swore you in at Fort Leavenworth and put you on a train and away you went?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you know anybody that you were sworn in with? On the train, did you know anybody else?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No. There was one boy who went with us at Leavenworth and he -- he found something wrong with him and he -- he got to go home and I went on.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So how did you get along in basic training with these southern boys and these guys from New York and these guys from California? You were a small-town Kansas boy.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, I got along pretty good because -- because I was -- I was a boxer and I was a 147-pound champion. I never lost a fight.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Is that right? You were a -- did you learn -- where did you learn to box, at home?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, home, and brothers.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you learned to box. And then, when you went in the Army, you were boxing?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Had you worked in the railroad before you went in the Army?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Where did you work?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: At Edgerton.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: At Edgerton on the Santa Fe?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Santa Fe. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So the minute they saw that on your record, they said, we're going to make a railroad man out this of this guy, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. They said they're needing people on the railroad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And they put us just ahead of everybody. Away we went.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you got out of basic and then they shipped you out right away, didn't they, to Europe?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes. We went to -- on a train to -- got on the boat. Took 13 days going across Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You didn't get seasick, did you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, but a lot of them did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: This small-town boy from Kansas, you'd never seen the ocean, had you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And 13 days. Were you in a convoy with other ships?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, they -- and they dodged German.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So they zigzagged back and forth --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We zigzagged back and forth.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- to keep away from the German submarines?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Mm-hmm. Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So did you -- where did you sleep, down below in the ship, or were you on deck?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We was down below. They -- they made the pineapple boat into ...

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: A troop carrier kind of thing --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: A troop carrier.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Had to eat standing up.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Eat standing up?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Lots of -- lots of soldiers --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Five boat -- five bunks high.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You weren't on the top one, were you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, I was on the bottom, thank goodness.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So were there a lot of troops on that ship? A lot of boys on that ship?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, it wasn't too big. It wasn't big as a lot of them, but it made -- we called it a pineapple boat and they just made it into a carrier.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Made it into a troop carrier?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Just five -- five bunks in a row, just all full.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And you -- where did you land?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Casablanca, North Africa.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Casablanca. And so the idea was you were going to be involved in the invasion of Europe when we went into Sicily in Europe, I guess, and Italy?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So were you --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We just took over railroad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. So what did you do? I mean, what was your job once you got to, let's say, Italy or Sicily on the -- and you were part of the 713th Railway Battalion, what was your job?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, I had to -- I was sergeant and I had 15 men and two corporals under me, and we helped anywhere we could. If somebody needed help before we was building the rail, well, we had to -- building bridges. We helped build bridges, too, and we supervised that to get things going.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So your job was to do anything that was necessary --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- to have the railroad move north so you could take supplies and men, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right, to keep things going, take gasoline and food. To get one line open to the front was our job.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you -- did you work long hours? I mean, was it more --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- than an eight-hour job?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, we were -- sometimes we'd -- we were in water up to our neck and -- yeah, we worked all kinds of hours to get something done.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And how many people altogether? You mentioned the ones that were in your crew, but did you have a lot of railroad, railway people?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They were all railroad people.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And how many did you have? Lots? I mean, hundreds?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We had four -- yeah. We had four companies of them. It was all -- all rail -- they were all railroad people but for different deals. And we -- I happen to be in the track.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you were laying track and --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- repairing track, I guess, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Where did you get the equipment, the locomotives and the cars?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They shipped them over. And we had different companies. Four -- four companies made a battalion. And I was in A Company. In fact, I've got a book there, Patty.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. We'll take a look at that in a little bit. So you were in A Company?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: In the 713th?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And you were in charge of track?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Laying track, repairing track?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They'd give us so -- so much territory to patrol and then keep going. And the Germans might blow it up during the night. They had a deal big enough to hook on the engine and run it on the track, and that deal could break them ties right in the middle. I got a picture of it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Is that right, the Germans had something like that?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, and we was close enough to the front that we just took -- when they did that, we just took a bulldozer and trucks could run on that chat and just blended that out a little bit, and they took supplies up there because the rails was no good with the ties broke. I think I got a picture of that in one of my books here.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, we'll look at that. Were you close to the front almost all the time?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, we got within pretty close. We could hear the guns all night.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you ever come under fire from anti-air -- excuse me, artillery or mortars?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Not -- not directly, but we were always close enough that that sound would lull you to sleep, anti—aircraft.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were you ever strafed by --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- German airplanes or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, but they -- they come in and strafed our -- we had a ...

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, the rail yards?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Rail yards.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They'd do that. They caught us in there one time, and it wasn't too good.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Was the -- well, tell me about that time when they caught you there. You said it wasn't too good.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, what they do, they'd come in from Mount Vesuvius, and that was that -- oh ...

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, it was a mountain there in --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- Southern Italy, yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And they'd locate that. They'd been there. We'd run them out and then they'd cut their motor, and they'd drift in and be in that rail yard before everybody knew it, and it was pretty touchy.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So they'd bomb the -- bomb you and strafe you because they wanted to obviously --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- disrupt the railroad?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Shine, did -- did the rail that you were using, was it the same gauge wide as a US, or was --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Some of it was. And they had -- they had some little stuff, narrow gauge, they called it. And -- but the other was the same, same as ours.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So of course cars couldn't go on both, so --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, no, they had to have different wheels on it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, on the cars?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. But we got to shipping some stuff over from the States to -- took over. And the Frenchmen, they runnin' their trains, they -- they lost a lot of time. And we just took theirs away from them and run it. And sometime take -- take them a day or two to run what we run in half a day with our trains. And so they put -- they put us doing it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were you ever a -- on the part of a railroad crew, you know, fireman, engineer, brakeman --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- conductor, something --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, no, they were separate.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: They were separate?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, they were C Company.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: C Company, yeah?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: I was A Company. I was track builder --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: -- and bridge builder.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You got it to where they could go up there and then they took it up there?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, and ?Agent S? was headquarters and supply. That was the whole battalion. And I was A Company. It was track builder, and A -- C Company was for engineers and firemen.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Sure. Sure. Did we lose a lot of -- of cars and engines?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: They'd bomb them, is that what they would do or?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We bombed a lot of theirs, too. Yeah, it -- it wasn't too good, but we -- it had to be done.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yes, it did. How long were you there? More than a year in Europe --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Just long enough to get it -- get it fixed and then we'd go -- landed in Casablanca, been to Italy, France, and Germany. We went through the whole bunch.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, so wherever you were needed --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- you went as a --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- as a railway battalion?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We was 711th and other -- other guys with 727th, and we were noted for the two best outfits. And if they needed something, they'd call us to come up there and fix it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What was the -- looking back on it, it was a long time ago, but what's the worst day you spent in the railway service in Europe? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, no, I can't remember the worst day because I had a lot of them.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You had a lot of bad days, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, but we -- we'd come through it okay. Yeah, and they had a lot of -- they had some rails, them Germans had rails 128—foot long underground. And we found them and we -- we pulled them out with bulldozers and pulled them out and used them.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Used their own stuff against them, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Now, were you over there until the -- until the Germans gave up --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes, that was terrible. They come in givin' -- with their hands up, old men, 45 and 50 years old, and little boys not over 16 or 17 years old; had holes in their -- their shoes wore out and they were just terrible.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: It was cold in the wintertime, too --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and they probably hadn't been -- they weren't eating very well, I'm sure of that.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, they were give up by the thousands when the war was over. And they -- they were even using horse equipment to -- for some of their artillery.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, tell me about the day that you captured some German paratroopers.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, this old guy, old Frenchman, he had a horse and buggy. And he come in our outfit and he said, tedeschi; that was German. And he said they stealed his food. And there was four paratroopers, and one of them was dressed like an Arab, and he was stealing the old man's food. And he figured he was going to die anyhow, so he -- he come in and told us. Well, us sergeants, we jumped at that. We grabbed our rifles and the captain went with us. And they were in a wheat field and they had some trees up there and they were in that shade of that -- them trees. And we sneaked up on him and we got as -- we got as close as you're across the street there to them. And we all raised up and _____+ hands -- and this one had been asleep, he rubbed his eyes, great big 'ol boy, and he -- first thing he said, was, Have you got automobile? And our captain said, you asked me, if you can't walk, we'll plant you right here. Uh-oh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So he started walking, did he?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, he started walking real quick. And then we turned them over to the right -- right people and went on in our business. But we got that citation from General Gray.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: We're going to show a picture of that in a minute. So probably toward the end of the war they were fighting with old men and young boys --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and were poorly equipped, weren't they?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, it was terrible and -- and they had so much propaganda going on and they -- they thought they were winning. A lot of them women would say, How did we lose the war? How did we lose the war? But that's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, when you were -- when you'd go into small towns, as you would, I'm sure, when you're following the rail line north or wherever it went, how did the German people react to you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, most of them were real good. Most of them -- most of them were real good. Of course, when -- when we first took over, we weren't even allowed to say hello to them gals. And it was that bad. And then, like that -- well, like I told you, I got in that pellet point bunch, I had 103 points, and we got to come by boat, home. And there was a battalion that come in there, tank battalion, and their emblem was the Great Speckled Bird. And they -- they had the yard arm up on the ship. And this point bunch, we'd come in on the same deal. Well, we'd give a sailor five dollars for a bed sheet and he painted old Sad Sack on that bed sheet. And during the night one of the sailors went up and put that above the Great Speckled Bird. That old colonel come out there next morning looked up and said -- and we pulled his in camp, edge of camp -- and we -- running out there to get it. When they talked to him he had them chickens on his shoulders. And he said, you got stories, Colonel? He says, I don't have a damn word to say to these point men, this man will give you his toy. He just kept walking _____+

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, do you remember where you were when you heard the war was over?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, I was in -- I was on the way home. We were coming this way when I heard that. We thought we were going over there to ...

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You thought you were going to Japan?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, we thought we were going to Japan, and I was in -- one kid had -- he had a fit. He got so tickled he -- he had -- oh, I don't know what they call that when they get all --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Had the shakes?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. We were in the middle of the Atlantic when we got word that -- that it was over.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yeah, because you had a lot of points, didn't you, because you'd been over there a long time?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: 103, I think -- I think it was.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So when you got back, when you got back to the United States, were you discharged right away, or did they send you someplace else?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No, we got to Fort Leavenworth, got discharged at Fort Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then sent you home, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, of course, I wasn't very far from there.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: No, you weren't far. You weren't far away. So when you got out of the service in '45?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Mm—hmm.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So what have you been -- what did you do then for the next almost 60 years? That was a long time ago when you got out.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, when I -- well, I went to work on the railroad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Back in Edgerton --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Water service department. I knew this old guy before I went in, and as a kid I'd go down there and watch him work and everything. And he said, Shine, when you grow up, he says, I want you to work for me. And by golly, I contacted him when I got back from the Army, and he said, I'll go to Ottawa next week, I can hire you. I got a place over there. And me and another guy was in the Navy in Normandy with me, we went over to Ottawa, and I worked a couple years there and then got laid off. And that's when I went up to the Navy.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you worked on the railroad -- before we go any farther, how did you get the nickname "Shine"?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: My oldest brother give me that. He called me Sunshine, and then it just dropped the "sun." I've been Shine ever since.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did they call you Shine in the Army?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Everybody called you Shine, huh?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, it was Shine. When I first went to vote, my teachers and stuff, they said, Shine, what is your real name? Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you've been Shine --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: I have.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- for 88 years?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So I guess you might as well hang onto it. That's great. So you worked on the railroad?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then you got laid off?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then -- then you joined the Navy?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Now, where was the Navy?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Olathe Naval Air Station.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay, just a few miles away from here --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- at the naval air station. They needed -- how did you happen to get in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And I was -- well, I seen this deal where you come up there and retain your rate and sports and everything else. And I went up and -- and they found out I had ten years Santa Fe. And the old commander said, you're in charge of the railroad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you were a railroad man after all?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Everybody got tickled about that.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you do any boxing --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- in the Navy, out there in Olathe?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Not -- not too much out there, but I went in the CCC camp, too, earlier.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: That was before you went in the Army?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, Civilian Conservation Corps, and I boxed in there and --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you were an undefeated boxer, were you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, I -- yeah, I had quite a title there at the CC camp. I whipped the boxing instructor.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Oh, you're not -- you're not supposed to beat the instructor. Where was the CCC camp?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Minnesota.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Up in Minnesota?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: We helped plant 10,000 acres of pine trees up there. We got 30 dollars a month and had to send 25 of it home. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you did a lot of boxing up there?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, and then in the Army.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And you boxed in the Army?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Fort Belvoir, Virginia, out by the engineer training center. And we didn't know when was going to be fighting. We'd run around with full field packs all day, and we'd go down there, and the sergeant might stick his head in the tent and say, hey, you're fighting over at ring three tonight. I said, oh, no.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And you'd put the gloves on and start swinging, hey?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, you said you were undefeated?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: I had four draws.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Four draws?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: But they run out of gas same time I did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Four draws and a lot of victories, and that's a great boxing record.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you're in charge of the railroad down in the Navy out in Olathe?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, it had got so bad that I went and told the commander. I said, Commander, this is in such bad shape, we're going to have to resurface the whole thing. And he said, would you be inspector for the government? I said, yes. And a guy named Novelli from Chicago, he got the contract. And he had a sergeant Louie Battista and he was doing good. And that goes clear to the railroad, you know. And he goes down there and he starts handling -- the deal said you had to have grade stakes. The Navy wanted grade stakes. And old Louie, he was running around there just perfect. I said, Louie, that won't fly, I said, you got to have grade stakes. He says, Jesus Christ, what are we going to do? Our surveyor's in Chicago. I said, well, you better get him. And old Novelli was a smart old duck. He said, I got to call Novelli. And he called him, and Novelli said, Louie, he says, take Peer over to the Ottawa, he knows all those railroad people, and he'll get you a guy to run the profile on that track. And that's what we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you were -- the Navy was satisfied and you got the job done right?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And you stayed in the Navy then until you had 20 years service?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Mm—hmm.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then you retired out of the Army and out of the Navy with 20 years military service?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What did you do then?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, then I went over Richards-Gebaur Air Force Base, and then I come back to Olathe, and they closed it. And I was going to retire. That's when I went up with the Indians at that Lawrence, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So you worked at the college, Haskell --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Haskell Junior College.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- Institute?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And fact, I got a deal here just the other day for -- to come up for dinner, Christmas.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, I think you ought to.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They invite me over.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: That's good. That's good. So you had -- you had a very interesting military career?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yes, I did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Both in the Army and in the Navy. Not -- not too many guys can say they worked on the railroad, and you're up during World War II. And captured some German paratroopers?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Came back and served your time in the Navy and then had civil service work --

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and retired?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: And then, too, when I was at the Navy, I coached -- I was coach and player on the baseball team. We played in the semi-pro league in Kansas City, and we had a lot of fun.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were you a pretty good player, pretty good ball player?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Probably was. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Played shortstop and could pitch a little bit.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You think you could go out today and pitch a little bit?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Oh, if I had to.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: We're not going to ask you to today. It's kind of cold outside.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, might hurt the arm.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: We don't want your arm to go. Well, let's -- I take a picture of some of the things that you've got here. What is the story on Anzio Annie, this gun?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: They would shoot several rounds and then pull the gun away in a tunnel, and the Germans didn't know where it was coming from. And that's -- it shows it in transport here.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How long was that gun?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: It was on two flatcars. It took two flatcars to haul it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: It took two flatcars. And how far would it shoot?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Thirty miles.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Thirty miles. Man, that was a big gun, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: It was.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And here you are in 1941. So here's some of Shine's medals and souvenirs that his daughter put together, a very nice board that shows his sergeant stripes, his outfit emblem. Got the Ruptured Duck there when he got discharged and then his medals. Very nice. This is a book about Shine's battalion, the 713th Railway Battalion, and the Company A that he was in. And I believe there's a picture of you inside. Let's look at it. So here's Shine. He's giving some candy to a little French girl. What's the story there, Shine?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Well, she's taking them clothes to her mother.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Ah, her mother did your laundry for you?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, that was nice.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: She called me Sergeanta Peer.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Sergeanta Peer? She didn't call you Shine?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Oh, that's a nice picture. Long time ago. Sixty years ago.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So here's a citation given to Sergeant Shine Peer for his participation in capturing several Germans that Shine has told us about it. And you can read it. Very nice. Shine -- [Video interruption]

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Spiking Their Guns.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Spiking Their Guns. That is the insignia of the Santa Fe Battalion?

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: 713th Railway Battalion, World War II, serving in North Africa and all through Europe.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And the motto, we'll zoom in on that, is "Spiking Their Guns." Very, very nice. So here's Shine with his daughter, Patty, who lives not too far from here. And a great big extended family. Patty, you have six children, I believe?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And how many grandchildren do you have?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Seven.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Seven. So you'd have seven great grandchildren and the oldest one is how old now?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Thirty, and the youngest one is 17.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: The youngest one is 17. That is a beautiful family. Here's a picture of whole tribe taken about how long ago, seven or eight years?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah, probably about five years ago, maybe.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: About five years ago. That is a wonderful family. and Shine, I believe your wife passed away a year ago and you'd been married 57 years. So not only -- you had a great military career, served in both the Army and the Navy, a great civilian career, retired from civil service, and retired -- you're a 20-year-man in the military, and a wonderful family. And I'm glad I can get a picture of you and your daughter, Patty, who lives close by. Shine, I want to thank you very much for this interview, and I want to thank you for what you did for our country.

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You're welcome. And I bet you could still sling a little leather if you had to?

sp.speaker: Raymond C. Peer
sp.p: Yeah. I think so.
